 Judgment
Subham Aggarwal Vs. State 1

By this judgment I will dispose of appeal u/sec.374 Cr.PC. filed on behalf of convict Subham Gupta against the judgment dated 22.08.2014 and order on sentence dated 29.08.2014 passed by Sh. Gaurav Rao, Ld. ACMM-II, Patiala House Court, New Delhi.
2 The brief facts of the case as per record and from trial court record are that accused is running an establishment namely M/s Shri Ganga Ji Traders at B-6, Nehru Vihar, Delhi-110094.

On 21.10.2002 at about 6.15 p.m. Food Inspector Sh. Ram Prakash visited the said place and purchased 750 grams R/O C-36/4 vs The State (Govt. Of Nct Of Delhi) on 3 August, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/153901836/
1 of "Dal Arhar"
from accused.
FI was accompanied with SDM/LHA Sh. Anil Banka.
The said Arhar Dal was purchased for the purposes of analysis under PFA Act.
The same sample was divided into three parts, packed as per Rules of PFA.
Panchanama was prepared.
One sample was sent for analysis to Public Analyst.
As per the report of Analyst, sample did not confirm to the standard because "The sample is adulterated because it is coloured with synthetic colouring matter viz. Tartrazine."
3 As the sample was failed, prosecution was launched by Food Inspector by filing complaint dated 25.10.2004 with the court.
Accused was summoned.
He has exercised his right u/sec.13(2) PFA Act to get the sample analyzed by CFL.

CFL reported "I am of the opinion that the sample bearing no.
AB/LHA/3341 does not Subham Aggarwal Vs. State conform to standards of split pulse (Dal) Arhar as per PFA Rules, 1955 (Synthetic colour Tartrazine detected)."
4

Charge was framed against accused u/sec.2(ia) (a) (j)
(m) read with sec.7 of PFA Act, 1954 punishable u/sec.16(1A) of PFA Act.
5

After trial, vide judgment dated 22.08.2014 accused was convicted for offence u/sec.16(1A) of PFA Act and vide order on sentence dated 29.08.2014, accused was directed to undergo simple imprisonment for a period of 18 months and fine of Rs.10,000/- and in default of payment of fine SI of 60 days.

6 In this appeal, the accused has assailed the judgment on the following grounds:-
(i) Non-compliance of Sec.10(7) of PFA Act and Rule i.e. independent witnesses were not joined.
(ii) Non-compliance of Rule 14 of PFA Rules i.e. the bottles, jhawa, polythene were not made clean and dried at the spot by the food inspector or any other official.
(iii) Appellant is protected in view of Sec.19(2) PFA as he had established that he purchased the sample commodity from some other person and sold the same in the same condition.
7 No reply was filed by respondent/state and the matter was argued orally.
8 I h a v e g o n e t h r o u g h t h e r e c o r d , T r i a l C o u r t r e c o r d a n d
Subham Aggarwal Vs. State have heard the submissions of Ld. counsel for appellant and Ld. SPP for State.
9 It is argued by counsel for appellant that no public witness was present in the proceedings nor efforts were made to join any public witnesses.

As far as this argument is concerned, the same R/O C-36/4 vs The State (Govt. Of Nct Of Delhi) on 3 August, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/153901836/
2 argument was raised before the Ld. Trial Court.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The same was dealt by the trial court from para 23 to 28 of the judgment.

As far as opinion/finding of the trial court regarding this argument is concerned, I do not find any infirmity in those findings and the same are upheld and the arguments regarding this fact does not find any force and thus rejected.
10 It is further argued that compliance u/sec.14 PFA Rules was not proved on record by the prosecution.
It is stated that witnesses are deposing differently with respect to the cleanliness of jhaba etc.
It is further stated that it was the duty of the prosecution to prove these facts.
These arguments were also addressed before the trial court.
The relevant part of the judgment dealing with these arguments are from para 29 to 47 of the judgment.
From the perusal of the record, it appears that prosecution was able to state that the bottles, jhaba, the polythene used for weighing the sample commodity was clean.
There is no other fact on record.

So, in these circumstances, the prosecution w a s a b l e t o p r o v e t h a t c o m p l i a n c e u / s e c . 1 4 o f P F A A c t w a s  Subham Aggarwal Vs. State properly done and the relevant portion of the judgment is thus upheld.
11 It is further argued that accused had purchased the sample commodity from Shankar Lal Shri Ram, 4101, Naya Bazar, Delhi, vide bill no. 15827 dated 19.10.2002 Ex.DW1/A.

It is stated that on account of Sec.19(2) PFA Act, accused is protected against prosecution as it has established that the commodity was purchased from some other person and sold in the same condition.

This leg of arguments were dealt by the court from para 106 to 111.
12
As far as the arguments in this regard is concerned, the law discussed by the trial court is correct and the same is self explanatory.
However, as far as the analysis of facts are concerned, to my opinion, the same requires some more elaboration.

13 From the perusal of the cross-examination of PW2 FI R. K. Bhaskar dated 17.09.2009 he admitted that the bill Ex.DW1/A when shown to the seller i.e. M/s Shankar Lal Sri Ram, he deposed "it is correct that during investigation, FI Suniti Kumar Gupta had received a letter from the accused along with the copy of the bill and on that basis letter was issued to the supplier.

It is correct that the supplier in his reply admitted the bill and the sale Subham Aggarwal Vs. State to the vendor and also enclosed copy of the bill of M/s Dwarka Rice & General Mill, Mark X-1, but added that he is not responsible for sale of Dal in loose condition."
14
It is further argued that accused had purchased the sample commodity from Shankar Lal Shri Ram, 4101, Naya Bazar, Delhi vide bill Ex.DW1/A.

It is stated that on account of Sec.19(2) PFA Act,
accused is protected against prosecution as it has established that the commodity was purchased from some other person and sold in the same condition.
This leg of arguments were dealt by the court from para 95 to 100.

15 On the other hand, it is argued by Ld. APP for State that the star witness cited by the defence i.e.
DW1 had denied that the sample commodity was not that which was sold by him to accused.
So, in these circumstances accused cannot get benefit u/sec.19 (2) PFA Act.

R/O C-36/4 vs The State (Govt. Of Nct Of Delhi) on 3 August, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/153901836/
3 16
From the perusal of testimony of DW1, he had admitted that bill Ex.DW1/A was issued by his firm in favour of M/s Ganga Ji Traders.
Similarly, DW2 had stated that he has purchased the Dal from M/s Shankar Lal Shri Ram.
However, during cross-examination of DW1 he had stated "it is correct that as per my knowledge the sample was lifted from Ganga Ji Traders from an open and loose bag without any declaration.
The sample Subham Aggarwal Vs. State  commodity which was lifted from the accused did not belong to me as it was lying in unsealed and unbranded condition at the time of lifting the sample".
17 It is argued by Ld. counsel for State that DW1 has specifically stated that the sample commodity was not sold by him but he has sold some other lot of Dal Arhar.
On the other hand, it is submitted by counsel for accused that the sample was taken from the same Dal which was bought by the accused from DW1.
18 As far as these arguments are concerned, we have to go to the scheme of PFA and the scheme of warranty as mentioned in Sec.19(2) of PFA Act.

As per Sec.19(2) PFA Act, if the vendor remain able to prove that he has purchased the sample commodity, on bill, from a supplier and sold it in the same condition as bought from supplier, he is exempted from prosecution.
However, then the prosecution/culpability get passed to the supplier.
So, there is a unique situation in which the supplier is hanging i.e. there is conflict of interest.

So, if supplier admits the bill by which the adulterated commodity is sold to the vendor and vendor is able to prove that he sold/stored the same commodity, then he exposes himself for criminal liability.
In normal parlance he will avoid to do the same.

Subham Aggarwal Vs. State

Moreover PW2 in his cross-examination has stated "it is correct that the supplier in his reply admitted the bill and the sale to the vendor and also enclosed copy of the bill of M/s Dwarka Rice & General Mill, Mark X-1, but added that he is not responsible for sale of Dal in loose condition".
20 From the statement of PW2, DW1 and DW2, it is admitted case that some Dal Arhar was purchased from M/s Shankar Lal Shri Ram.
However, Shankar Lal Shri Ram refused to accept the liability on the ground that he is not responsible if the commodity is sold in loose condition.
In his testimony before this court also he has stated that the commodity was sold in loose condition.

Now,
from where DW1 gained the knowledge that the commodity was sold in loose condition, is not disclosed.
He can not be privy to the information regarding the manner of sampling.
So, this appears that he cannot depose to these facts as it can be presumed that he was not having knowledge of sampling done on the date of sampling.
Hence, these facts deposed by DW1 cannot damage the case of DW2.
21 So, it can be concluded that the sample commodity was purchased by the accused from DW1 through Ex.DW1/A. 22

It is argued that the sample commodity was taken from an open gunny bag and was not stored in its original condition and Subham Aggarwal Vs. State thus benefit u/sec.19(2) PFA Act cannot be extended to accused.
R/O C-36/4 vs The State (Govt. Of Nct Of Delhi) on 3 August, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/153901836/
4 23

As far as Sec.19(2) PFA Act is concerned, the same is as follows:-
"19(2)-A Vendor shall not be deemed to have committed an offence pertaining to the sale of any adulterated or misbranded articles of food if he proves:-
(a) that he purchased the article of food- (i) in a case where a license is prescribed for the sale thereof, from a duly licensed manufacturer, distributor or dealer,
(ii) in any other case, from any manufacturer, distributor or dealer, with a written warranty in the prescribed form; and (b) that the article of food while in his possession was properly stored and that he sold it in the same state as he purchased it."
So, Sec. 19(2) PFA Act is exception to the general rule.
However the onus is upon the accused to make out its case in Sec.19(2) PFA Act.
So, he has to prove that he has bought the sample commodity from a supplier and second the said commodity was stored in the same condition as that bought from the supplier.

24 Now whether the mere opening of the stitched sack/container and taking out the commodity alters its condition and takes the case out of the purview of Sec.19(2) of PFA Act, is dealt by Superior Courts.

In A. P. Grain and Sweets Merchant Association Vs. Union of India, WP NO. 468/69, DOD 31.03.1970 in para 13, it is laid down as follows"-
 Subham Aggarwal Vs. State "The argument of counsel for petitioners that the provision that a retail seller who opens a container of a branded article of food loses even the limited protection under section 19(2) is without substance.

entities.text: A. P. Grain and Sweets Merchant Association Vs. Union of India, WP NO. 468/69, DOD 31.03.1970
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Clause (b) of subj-section (2) of section 19 does not prove nor does it imply, that if the container of a branded article is opened, the article of food ceases to be in the same state in which the vendor purchased it.

If the article of foods is sold in the same condition in which it was purchased from a licensed manufacturer or dealer, or was purchased with a warranty, the vendor will not lose the protection of sub-section (2) of section 19 merely because he opened the container.

If the vendor has obtained the article from a licensed manufacture, distributor or from a manufacture, distributor or dealer, he is protected, provided he has properly stored the article and sells it in the same state as he purchased the article, even if it turns out that the article was adulterated or misbranded."
So, accordingly, the retailer can sell the article by opening the container/bag but with condition that he should have stored the article in the same condition as it was purchased from supplier.
25 Now as per DW2 he has stated "I had not made any adulteration and I sold the same to the FI in the same condition in which I had purchased it."
There is no cross-examination on this aspect as to whether the Dal was in the same condition as bought or there was any change of condition.

R/O C-36/4 vs The State (Govt. Of Nct Of Delhi) on 3 August, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/153901836/
5 26

As far as the reasoning given by the trial court in para 111 (starting from secondly) is concerned vis-a-vis the status of Subham Aggarwal Vs. State vendor and supplier, the same is on wrong footing with respect to the law laid down by Superior Courts.

entities.text: Subham Aggarwal Vs. State vendor and supplier
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In Aboo Vs. FI, 2003 (1) FAC 81 and FI Vs. M. H. Shoukathali, 1989 (1) FAC 261, Hon. High Court of Kerala had stated "But the question whether by opening its package the "state" of the food article would be disturbed or changed.

entities.text: FI Vs. M. H. Shoukathali, 1989 (1) FAC 261
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: S. 19(2) is primarily intended to give protection to the retail dealers.
If a retailer is not permitted to sell the article in retail after he purchases it from a wholesale dealer it would affect the trading system of retail business.
One of the usual modes of retail business is to buy articles in bulk and sell them in smaller quantities.

The Legislature would never have intended that the retailer would be permitted to avail the defence envisaged in S.19(2) only if he sells the food article in the same package or container without opening them.
There cannot be a hard and fast rule that every article is liable to change its state when it is disinterred from its container.
Coriander is certainly not that type of article which undergoes transformation through disinterment from its package.
No cereals or other edible grains would lose its state, in normal conditions, by its exposure from the packages."
So, in these circumstances, the reasoning given by the trial court is erroneous and contrary to the law laid down in this regard.
Hence, the same is reversed in terms of the aforesaid two judgments of Hon. Kerala High Court.
Subham Aggarwal Vs. State
So, in these circumstances, accused is able to prove that he has purchased the commodity/sample commodity from the supplier.
He sold the commodity in the same condition as when bought from the supplier and has not done any adulteration.
27 So, in these circumstances, accused is able to prove that he is exempted by the provisions of warranty as mentioned in Sec.19(2) PFA Act.
28 So, the judgment and order on sentence of the trial court is reversed.
29 Accused Subham Aggarwal is acquitted of the charges u/sec.16(1A) read with sec.7 of PFA Act.
30 Bail Bond u/sec.437A Cr.P.C. already furnished.
Accepted for six months.
31 TCR be sent back with copy of the order.
32 File of appeal be consigned to Record Room.
